lesson.title: A Day in Madrid: Reading
lesson.subtitle: Connected narrative in Madrid combining ser/estar, preterite/imperfect, gustar, and object pronouns

hook.title: Morning to Night in Madrid
hook.content:
Follow the story of a day in Madrid and watch how every tense and verb choice tells part of the story:
• *Por la mañana me levanté a las ocho.* (Preterite dot: I got up at eight.)
• *El día era hermoso y el café estaba caliente.* (Imperfect background: The day was beautiful and the coffee was hot.)
• *Visité a mi mejor amigo y comí en un restaurante central.* (Personal 'a' + preterite events.)
• *¡La visita fue un éxito y me encanta esta ciudad!* (Preterite verdict fue + inverted encantar!)

pattern.title: Reading for Structure and Meaning
pattern.content: Notice how era describes the day's ongoing quality, estaba describes the coffee's temperature state, and fue judges the whole completed visit as a success!

exercises.prompt: Match each English expression with its Spanish partner:

matching_pairs.english: the day was beautiful (ongoing background trait)
the coffee was hot (ongoing past state)
the visit was a success (verdict on completed event)
I spoke with my best friend

exercises.target_answer: el día era hermoso, el café estaba caliente, la visita fue un éxito, hablé con mi mejor amigo, me encanta esta ciudad mágica
exercises.meaning: the day was beautiful (ongoing background trait), the coffee was hot (ongoing past state), the visit was a success (verdict on completed event), I spoke with my best friend, I love this magical city
exercises.explanation: era, estaba, and fue each play their distinct role in a past narrative.

exercises.prompt: In 'El día era hermoso, el café estaba caliente y la cena fue fantástica', why do all three English 'was' clauses use a different Spanish verb?
options: Because día, café, and cena have different genders
era = ongoing past characteristic (ser); estaba = ongoing past thermal state (estar); fue = final verdict on a completed past event (preterite of ser)!
exercises.target_answer: era = ongoing past characteristic (ser); estaba = ongoing past thermal state (estar); fue = final verdict on a completed past event (preterite of ser)!
exercises.explanation: Spanish distinguishes essence vs state (ser vs estar) AND ongoing background vs completed event (imperfect vs preterite)!

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'Yesterday I spoke with my friend and ate at the restaurant'
exercises.target_answer: Ayer hablé con mi amigo y comí en el restaurante
exercises.meaning: Yesterday I spoke with my friend and ate at the restaurant
exercises.explanation: Ayer hablé con mi amigo y comí en el restaurante.

exercises.idea: say that the hotel was central and the city was beautiful (ongoing past descriptions with era)
cues: The hotel was central → El hotel era central
and the city was beautiful → y la ciudad era hermosa
idea_parts: The hotel was central → El hotel era central
and the city was beautiful → y la ciudad era hermosa
exercises.target_answer: El hotel era central y la ciudad era hermosa
exercises.meaning: The hotel was central and the city was beautiful
exercises.explanation: El hotel era central y la ciudad era hermosa.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Ayer fue un día mágico en Madrid
exercises.target_answer: Ayer fue un día mágico en Madrid
exercises.meaning: Yesterday was a magical day in Madrid
cues: a magical day: un día mágico
exercises.explanation: Ayer fue un día mágico en Madrid.

summary.outcome: Combine era, estaba, fue, hablé, comí, and me encanta in connected narrative passages.

use_example.german: El día era hermoso, el café estaba caliente y ayer fue un día mágico en Madrid.
use_example.english: The day was beautiful, the coffee was hot, and yesterday was a magical day in Madrid.

summary.takeaway: era = ongoing trait; estaba = ongoing state/location; fue = completed event verdict.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next ([3002] Trap Watch: False Friends in the Wild): test yourself against the full Spanish False Friends deck!

twist.prompt: Assemble: 'The coffee was hot and the cake was delicious'
twist.target_answer: El café estaba caliente y el pastel estaba rico
twist.explanation: Both hotness and tasting delicious are states, so both use estaba!

ciudad.etymology_derivation: Latin cīvitātem ('citizenship, city') gives English 'city' and 'civic', and Spanish ciudad.

hotel.etymology_derivation: Silent initial H. Latin hospitāle gives both 'hospital' and 'hotel'.

café.etymology_derivation: Turkish kahve → Italian caffè → Spanish café. An international word shared across Europe.

estaba.english_meaning: I / he / she / it was (imperfect of estar)

era.english_meaning: I / he / she / it was (imperfect of ser)
era.context_phrase: Cuando era joven, vivía en Madrid.
era.context_translation: When I was young, I lived in Madrid.
era.etymology_derivation: Latin erat — English 'era' (an ongoing epoch of time) is the exact same root!

fue.english_cognate: was / went (shared preterite of ser & ir!)
fue.shift_rule: Shared preterite of ser and ir (fui, fuiste, fue)
fue.etymology_derivation: ser ('to be') and ir ('to go') share the exact same preterite forms: fui ('I was / I went'), fue ('it was / he went')!

hablé.context_translation: Yesterday I spoke with my mother.
hablé.etymology_derivation: Notice how the accent mark carries the entire tense difference: hablo ('I speak') vs. habló ('he/she spoke')!

comí.context_translation: Yesterday I ate at that restaurant.

encantar.english_meaning: to love, be delighted by (me encanta: I love)
encantar.etymology_derivation: Literally 'it enchants me': me encanta (sg.), me encantan (pl.).

cion.name: The -CIÓN Passport
cion.phonetic_rule: English -tion /-(e)ʃən/ becomes Spanish -ción /-ˈθjon/. Always stressed on the ó, and 100% feminine (la).
cion.historical_linguistics: Descends from Latin third-declension abstract nouns in -tiō (accusative -tiōnem). English borrowed thousands via French; Spanish evolved -ción directly.
cion.philological_note: Because every single -ción noun is feminine, this family hands you grammatical gender for thousands of words without memorization.

dad.name: The -DAD Quality Bridge
dad.phonetic_rule: English abstract nouns in -ty correspond to Spanish -dad /-ˈdað/. 100% feminine (la).
dad.historical_linguistics: From Latin abstract quality nouns in -tās, accusative -tātem. Spanish lenited the intervocalic dental stop to -dad.
dad.philological_note: City (ciudad), reality (realidad), university (universidad). The ending guarantees feminine gender.

mente.name: The -MENTE Adverb Engine
mente.phonetic_rule: Feminine adjective + -mente /-ˈmente/ forms adverbs corresponding to English -ly.
mente.historical_linguistics: Originates from the Latin ablative phrase [adjective] mente ('with a ... mind'). Because mens is feminine in Latin, Spanish preserves the feminine adjective stem.
mente.philological_note: Notice how Spanish preserves the feminine form: exactamente (not exactomente). If the base adjective carries a tilde, it keeps it: fácilmente.

ar_engine.name: The -ar Verb Factory
ar_engine.phonetic_rule: English Latinate nouns in -ation correspond to Spanish first-conjugation infinitives in -ar /-ˈaɾ/.
ar_engine.historical_linguistics: Latin first-conjugation verbs in -āre. English borrowed the noun form; Spanish kept the verb stem alive.
ar_engine.philological_note: The 'celebrar trap': strip the entire -ation before attaching -ar. Celebración → celebrar (not celebratar).

ico.name: The -ICO Bridge
ico.phonetic_rule: English adjectives in -ic / -ical correspond to Spanish -ico /-iko/ (masculine) / -ica (feminine). Always carries a written accent on the antepenultimate syllable.
ico.historical_linguistics: Greek -ikos passed through Latin -icus. In Spanish, these are palabras esdrújulas and must be written with a tilde.
ico.philological_note: Mágico, público, básico, económico, romántico. The tilde tells your voice exactly where to jump.

al.name: The -AL Invariable Passport
al.phonetic_rule: English adjectives ending in -al match Spanish -al /-ˈal/ with identical spelling and gender-invariable singular form.
al.historical_linguistics: Latin adjectival suffix -ālis ('pertaining to'). Both languages kept the spelling; Spanish stresses the final syllable.
al.philological_note: El plan natural, la idea natural: no gender change in the singular.

f_to_h.name: Latin F- ➔ Silent H-
f_to_h.phonetic_rule: Latin initial f- weakened into an aspiration and became completely silent h- in Spanish, while English kept the Latin f- cognate.
f_to_h.historical_linguistics: Castilian contact with Basque/Cantabrian substrate languages lacking initial /f/ caused Latin /f-/ to weaken into silent h-.
f_to_h.philological_note: Hacer ↔ fact/manufacture; hijo ↔ filial; hierro ↔ ferrous; horno ↔ furnace. When you see a silent h-, think f.

ct_to_ch.name: Latin -CT- ➔ Spanish -CH-
ct_to_ch.phonetic_rule: Latin medial -ct- palatalized into Spanish -ch- /-tʃ-, while English kept the learned Latin -ct- form.
ct_to_ch.historical_linguistics: The velar stop /k/ vocalized into a palatal glide [j] which then fused with the dental /t/ into the affricate /tʃ/.
ct_to_ch.philological_note: Noctem ➔ noche (nocturnal); lactem ➔ leche (lactose); factum ➔ hecho (fact); octō ➔ ocho (octave).

pl_cl_fl_to_ll.name: Latin PL-/CL-/FL- ➔ Spanish LL-
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.phonetic_rule: Latin initial consonant clusters pl-, cl-, fl- palatalized into Spanish ll- /ʎ/ (or /ʝ/).
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.historical_linguistics: The initial stop or fricative conditioned progressive palatalization of the liquid /l/ in Western Iberian Vulgar Latin.
pl_cl_fl_to_ll.philological_note: Clāmāre ➔ llamar (claim/clamor); clāvis ➔ llave (clef/clavicle); pluvia ➔ lluvia (pluvial); plēnus ➔ lleno (plenty).
